note: Recorded sample output for demos and tests. Written for the medication-reminders sample brief; competitor details come from general product knowledge and were not re-checked on the web.

events.name: Agent
events.summary: competitors: medication reminder apps and alternatives

problem.statement: Adults managing several daily medications, for themselves or a parent, lose track of what has been taken and when, which leads to missed or doubled doses.
problem.context: Schedules change after doctor visits, doses vary by time of day, and carers often live apart from the person they support. Current tools remind but rarely help when plans change or when someone else needs to know a dose was taken.
whoIsAffected: Adults taking three or more medications a day
Adult children or partners who help manage someone else's medications
Older adults with low vision or limited dexterity
currentAlternatives: Phone calls or messages between carer and parent
constraints: No medical advice or dosage recommendations
Must be usable by older adults with low vision or limited dexterity
A carer may only follow someone with that person's consent
successSignals: Most scheduled doses are marked taken, skipped or snoozed rather than left unanswered
New users add their first medication in under a minute
Carers check in less often by phone because the app tells them what they need
Schedule changes are made in the app instead of on paper

competitors.name: Medisafe
competitors.summary: Dedicated medication reminder app with dose tracking and an optional supporter who is notified about missed doses.
strengths: Mature, focused reminder and tracking flow
Supporter concept is close to the carer use case
weaknesses: Broad feature set can make simple tasks feel busy
Some features sit behind a paid tier
notablePatterns: Supporter is alerted only when a dose is missed, not on every dose

competitors.name: MyTherapy
competitors.summary: Free medication reminder and health journal combining doses with measurements and symptoms.
strengths: Combines reminders with a simple health diary
weaknesses: Diary features add steps for people who only want reminders
notablePatterns: Daily to-do list framing of doses

competitors.name: Apple Health (Medications)
competitors.summary: Built-in iPhone health app that includes medication lists, schedules and logging.
strengths: Integrates with the wider Health app
weaknesses: iPhone only, so mixed-platform families can't share
Medications are one feature among many in Health
notablePatterns: Logging from the notification without opening the app

competitors.name: Phone clock alarms
competitors.summary: Many people simply set repeating alarms, labelled with the medication name.
strengths: Already on every phone, no setup to learn
weaknesses: No record of whether a dose was taken
Painful to update when a schedule changes
Nothing for a carer to see
notablePatterns: Labels on alarms used as a makeshift dose list

personas.name: The juggling self-manager
personas.context: Takes four to six medications at different times of day, works, and has a schedule that changes every few months after check-ups.
goals: Never wonder whether a dose was already taken
Update the plan quickly after a doctor's visit
frustrations: Re-entering a whole schedule when one dose changes
behaviours: Keeps an organiser at home and a few pills in a bag
personas.basisNote: No user research was uploaded. Based on the brief and on patterns in competitor products; validate with interviews.

personas.name: The remote carer
personas.context: An adult child who lives apart from a parent and helps manage their medications by phone and occasional visits.
goals: Know the evening dose was taken without calling
Be told when something is missed, not on every dose
frustrations: Learning about missed doses days later
behaviours: Checks in by phone or message
personas.basisNote: No user research was uploaded. Derived from the brief's carer requirement; validate with carers.

personas.name: The independent older adult
personas.context: Manages their own medications, has some loss of vision and finds small touch targets hard to use.
goals: Answer a reminder with one clear tap
frustrations: Apps that change layout after updates
behaviours: Prefers routines that stay the same
personas.basisNote: No user research was uploaded. Based on the brief's accessibility constraint; validate with older users.

jobs.situation: a reminder goes off while I'm busy
jobs.outcome: keep an accurate record without stopping what I'm doing

jobs.situation: my doctor changes one of my doses
jobs.motivation: update just that medication from a given date
jobs.outcome: trust that tomorrow's reminders are right

jobs.situation: it's evening and I haven't heard from my parent
jobs.motivation: see whether today's doses were taken
jobs.outcome: only call when something is actually wrong

jobs.situation: I can't remember if I took my morning pill
jobs.motivation: check today's history at a glance

insights.insight: Alarms remind but don't remember: people still can't tell later whether a dose was taken.
insights.implication: Every reminder should end in an explicit taken / skipped / snoozed answer, and today's view should show those answers clearly.

insights.insight: Carer apps that notify on every dose risk becoming noise; alerting on missed doses respects both people.
insights.implication: Default carer notifications to missed or skipped doses, with a calm daily summary available on demand.

insights.insight: Schedules change often, and editing a whole plan to change one dose is where people give up and go back to paper.
insights.implication: Make 'change from a date' a first-class action on a single medication, keeping history intact.

insights.insight: Older adults and people in a hurry both need one obvious action per reminder.
insights.implication: Large, clearly labelled primary actions; minimum 44–48 pt targets; text that scales with system settings.

hmw.question: How might we make answering a reminder a single, confident tap?
How might we let carers feel reassured without watching every dose?
How might we make a schedule change feel as easy as telling a friend?
How might we help someone check today's doses in under five seconds?

assumptions: Most target users already rely on phone notifications for reminders
Carers want alerts about missed doses rather than every dose
Schedule changes after check-ups are frequent enough to design for
Older users will accept an app if it stays simple and predictable
openQuestions: How do carers and the people they support want consent to work, and how is it withdrawn?
How long after a missed reminder should a carer be alerted?
Do people need to record pills taken outside the schedule (as-needed doses) in the first release?
Which accessibility settings do target users actually use day to day?
